extracted.intended_audience: journalists, researchers, and informed public interested in fact-checking methodologies
extracted.subtask_description: Compare and summarize the selection, research, and claim-evaluation methodologies used by major U.S. fact-checking organizations (PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, and The Washington Post Fact Checker). Focuses on how claims are chosen, investigated, and rated.

rubrics_metrics.name: PolitiFact — Selection questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adair says PolitiFact asks these critical questions when determining what to fact check:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted questions: "Is the statement rooted in a fact that is verifiable? We don’t check opinions, and we recognize that in the world of speechmaking and political rhetoric, there is license for hyperbole. Is the statement leaving a particular impression that may be misleading? Is the statement significant? We avoid minor 'gotchas' on claims that obviously represent a slip of the tongue. Is the statement likely to be passed on and repeated by others? Would a typical person hear or read the statement and wonder: Is that true?" (Use these questions to weed out opinions, trivial slips, or claims unlikely to be repeated; prioritize verifiable, potentially misleading, significant, and widely-disseminated statements.)

rubrics_metrics.name: PolitiFact — Newsworthiness and curiosity in selection
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact selects "the most newsworthy and significant" claims and is "guided by news judgement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PolitiFact also cites curiosity as a factor: staff may choose to check things they are curious about or suspect are wrong. Editors emphasize journalistic news judgement over social-science sampling when choosing items to check.

rubrics_metrics.name: PolitiFact — Research: contact source and prohibition on off-record sources
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact's research generally begins with contacting the source of a claim; this step is required of PolitiFact writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PolitiFact prohibits the use of off-record sources. Contacting the claimant's office for clarification, data, or sources is standard practice and a required step in their workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: PolitiFact — Research: reliance on nonpartisan data and source transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers are encouraged to seek out nonpartisan data sources (e.g., Bureau of Labor Statistics, Congressional Budget Office) and PolitiFact publishes a list of its sources with each article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PolitiFact uses news articles, subscription and free internet sources, and on-record interviews with reporters and experts to interpret data; they emphasize on-record sourcing and public, nonpartisan datasets; every article includes a sources list.

rubrics_metrics.name: PolitiFact — Claim-evaluation: editorial panel process
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead writer submits an article with a recommended rating to a panel of at least three editors; the panel evaluates the article and the author's recommended rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-making is collective: two of three panelists must agree on the final ruling (unanimity preferred). Meetings typically last 10–15 minutes but can extend for hours or require follow-ups. In extreme cases, an indecisive panelist may be replaced to reach a decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: PolitiFact — Truth-o-Meter rating system
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted definitions: "TRUE – The statement is accurate and there’s nothing significant missing. MOSTLY TRUE – The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information. HALF TRUE – The statement is partially accurate but leaves out important details or takes things out of context. MOSTLY FALSE – The statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression. FALSE – The statement is not accurate. PANTS ON FIRE – The statement is not accurate and makes a ridiculous claim." (Used to categorize overall veracity; panel assigns rating after discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: PolitiFact — Five principles guiding rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: Adair describes five principles the panel relies on when making rulings:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted principles: "Words matter -- We pay close attention to the specific wording of a claim. ... Context matters -- We examine the claim in the full context... Burden of proof -- People who make factual claims are accountable... Statements can be right and wrong -- We sometimes rate compound statements... Timing – Our rulings are based on when a statement was made and on the information available at that time." (Apply precise wording scrutiny, contextualization, burden on claimants, handling of compound statements, and time-bound evaluation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: FactCheck.org — Selection process: target and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: FactCheck.org targets "major U.S. political players in the form of TV ads, debates, speeches, interviews and news releases" and fact-checks social media and chain emails; it tends to avoid fact-checking media figures and pundits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The organization emphasizes verifiable facts, typically pursues claims that turn out to be false (stopping research early when a claim is true), and seeks claims with "national significance" that most readers would find interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: FactCheck.org — Research methods and sourcing norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Like its counterparts, FactCheck.org contacts the individual/organization responsible for a claim and traces claims back to original sources; it relies heavily on federal and state government agencies for raw data and uses nonprofit groups and think tanks as supplementary sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FactCheck.org makes regular use of experts to interpret data (but less than PolitiFact), compiles resource lists, avoids anonymous sources, and includes a list of sources at the end of each article. Former leadership frames their work as meeting high academic standards; anonymous sourcing is avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: FactCheck.org — Claim evaluation: no formal rating system; contextual, case-by-case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: FactCheck.org does not use an official rating system; its leadership calls rating systems "inflexible" and inherently subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted rationale: ratings like 'Pinocchios' are attention-grabbers but subjective, and many political claims don't fit neat categories. FactCheck.org favors a nuanced contextual analysis: refute egregious claims clearly but avoid systematized ratings that enable direct comparisons across claims and speakers; assessments are fluid and case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Washington Post Fact Checker — Selection principles and reader role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post's Fact Checker aims to "'truth squad' the statements of political figures regarding issues of great importance" and defines political figures broadly; it places heavy emphasis on reader tips for selecting claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles include: focus on verifiable facts (not opinion), concentrate on issues most important to voters (avoid nitpicking), and strive to be dispassionate and non-partisan. Readers are relied upon to suggest statements that need checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Washington Post Fact Checker — Research methods and preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post's Fact Checker reaches out to claimants and uses raw data and original sources; Kessler notes Google searches are effective for tracing figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike some peers, Kessler prefers not to consult subject experts routinely, preferring his own journalistic judgment; the Post will at times cite anonymous sources (unlike PolitiFact and FactCheck.org).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Washington Post Fact Checker — Claim-evaluation: 'reasonable man' standard and Pinocchio system
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post's Fact Checker uses a "'reasonable man' standard for reaching conclusions. We do not demand 100 percent proof." It employs the Pinocchio rating system (up to four Pinocchios) and additional symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pinocchio definitions: One Pinocchio: "Some shading of the facts...Some omissions and exaggerations... (you could view this as 'mostly true')." Two Pinocchios: "Significant omissions and/or exaggerations..." Three Pinocchios: "Significant factual error and/or obvious contradictions." Four Pinocchios: "Whoppers." Additional rules: repeated misstatements previously debunked can lead to higher Pinocchio ratings; a Geppetto check mark denotes true statements; an upside-down Pinocchio denotes 'flip-flops'; scales of justice denote claims too difficult to verify or requiring more time/data.
